result.markdown: --- title: "The standard error, derived in bands" description: "Casella and Berger get Var(X-bar) = sigma squared over n from one expansion and one substitution. Here every equation carries its own numbered R line, in seven bands — ending with the check, the plug-in, Efron's bootstrap, and why quartering the error needs quadrupling the sample." date: 2026-08-10 categories: - book-revisions tags: - standard error - variance - independence - bootstrap engine: knitr code-summary: "Show the working" --- ## Claim Casella and Berger prove $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2/n$ — Theorem 5.2.6(b), p. 214 — and stop there. The standard error is its square root. The proof is one idea. Square the deviation, expand the square into $n^2$ terms, take the expectation of each: the $n$ diagonal terms each expect $\sigma^2$, independence kills all $n(n-1)$ cross terms, and $n\sigma^2/n^2$ cancels once to $\sigma^2/n$. Nothing is estimated and no distribution is assumed. ## Code, maths, English ::: {.transition} | Code | Maths | English | |:--|:--|:--| | **BAND 1 — the three numbers** | | | | **L1 ↔ (1.1)** `mu <- 5` | (1.1) $\mu := 5$ | A definition, not a measurement: `<-` and $:=$ say the same thing. | | **L2 ↔ (1.2)** `sigma <- 1.3` | (1.2) $\sigma := 1.3,\quad\sigma^2 = 1.69$ | 1.3 cm of spread; 1.69 the same fact in cm². The square root between them is the whole post. | | **L3 ↔ (1.3)** `n <- 25` | (1.3) $n := 25$ | How many measurements: chosen, not estimated. | | **BAND 2 — one sample, and its deviations** | | | | **L4 ↔ (2.1)** `x <- rnorm(n, mu, sigma)` | (2.1) $X_1,\dots,X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ | 25 draws. The normal supplies independent numbers; no later line uses its shape. | | **L5 ↔ (2.2)** `z <- x - mu` | (2.2) $z_i := X_i - \mu,\qquad E[z_i] = 0$ | Centre on the **truth**, not on `mean(x)`; after this line $\mu$ is gone. | | **BAND 3 — the square splits into two blocks** | | | | **L6 ↔ (3.1)** `M <- outer(z, z)` | (3.1) $\Big(\sum_i z_i\Big)^2 = \sum_i z_i^2 + \sum_{i\ne j} z_i z_j$ | All 625 products of two deviations, in one 25×25 matrix. | | **L7 ↔ (3.2)** `sum(diag(M))` | (3.2) $\sum_i z_i^2 \quad$ — $n$ diagonal terms | prints 66.76 — *this* sample's block. Band 4 prints another number, and both are right. | | **L8 ↔ (3.3)** `sum(M) - sum(diag(M))` | (3.3) $\sum_{i\ne j} z_i z_j \quad$ — $n(n-1)$ cross terms | prints 160.7; with L7 that is 227.4 $=(\sum z_i)^2$, exactly. | | **L9 ↔ (3.4)** `n + n * (n - 1)` | (3.4) $n + n(n-1) = n^2$ | prints 625, the matrix's own cell count: $n$ squares, $n(n-1)$ crosses, nothing else. | | **BAND 4 — take the expectation of each block** | | | | **L10 ↔ (4.1)** `S <- matrix(rnorm(N * n, mu, sigma), N, n) - mu` | (4.1) $N$ independent samples of size $n$, each centred the same way | 100,000 repeats of band 2: an expectation, computed. | | **L11 ↔ (4.2)** `mean(rowSums(S^2))` | (4.2) $E\Big[\sum_i z_i^2\Big] = n\sigma^2$ | prints 42.28 ± 0.03782 against $n\sigma^2 = 42.25$. **L7's 66.76 was not an error**: the average is not the sample. | | **L12 ↔ (4.3)** `mean(rowSums(S)^2 - rowSums(S^2))` | (4.3) $E[z_iz_j] = \operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j) = 0,\quad i \ne j$ | prints 0.04796 ± 0.1851 against an exact 0. Independence enters here and nowhere else. | | **L13 ↔ (4.4)** `n * sigma^2` | (4.4) $n\sigma^2 = 42.25$ | 42.25 exactly — the algebra, before any data. | | **BAND 5 — add the blocks, divide by $n^2$, then root** | | | | **L14 ↔ (5.1)** `(1 / n^2) * (n * sigma^2)` | (5.1) $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) = \dfrac{1}{n^2}\,n\sigma^2 = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}$ | prints 0.0676 cm². One $n$ cancels out of $n\sigma^2/n^2$: that is Theorem 5.2.6(b). | | **L15 ↔ (5.2)** `sigma / sqrt(n)` | (5.2) $\operatorname{SE}(\bar X) = \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$ | prints 0.26 cm — (5.1) rooted, not interchangeable with it. | | **BAND 6 — check the finished result by simulation** | | | | **L16 ↔ (6.1)** `means <- replicate(N, mean(rnorm(n, mu, sigma)))` | (6.1) $\bar X_1,\dots,\bar X_N$ from $N$ independent samples | 100,000 averages of 25 fresh measurements: the experiment the theorem predicts. | | **L17 ↔ (6.2)** `var(means)` | (6.2) $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) \approx \widehat{\operatorname{var}}\big(\{\bar X_k\}\big)$ | prints 0.06734 against an exact 0.0676, ratio 0.9962: the averages land on (5.1). | | **L18 ↔ (6.3)** `sd(means)` | (6.3) $\operatorname{SE}(\bar X) \approx \widehat{\operatorname{sd}}\big(\{\bar X_k\}\big)$ | prints 0.2595 against 0.26 — (6.2) rooted and (5.2) agree to three digits. | | **BAND 7 — what the number is for** | | | | **L19 ↔ (7.1)** `sizes <- c(n, 4 * n, 16 * n)` | (7.1) $\operatorname{SE}(\bar X_n) = \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$, so $\operatorname{SE}_{4n} = \tfrac12 \operatorname{SE}_n$ and $\operatorname{SE}_{16n} = \tfrac14 \operatorname{SE}_n$ | No new derivation: the $\sqrt n$ of (5.2) read at $n$, $4n$, $16n$. | | **L20 ↔ (7.2)** `sd_sizes <- sapply(sizes, ...)` | (7.2) $\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}$ at each of the three sizes | prints 0.2589, 0.1297, 0.06467 against 0.26, 0.13, 0.065: quadrupling the sample halves the error (1.997 against 2, 4.003 against 4). Sixteen times the data buys a quarter, so halving again costs four times as much data. | | **L21 ↔ (7.3)** `se_hat <- sd(x) / sqrt(n)` | (7.3) $\widehat{\operatorname{SE}} = \dfrac{s}{\sqrt n}$, where $s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (X_i - \bar X)^2$ | prints 0.31 against a true 0.26. Not a bug: that sample's $s$ is 1.55 cm against $\sigma = 1.3$, so its honest bar is wider. | | **L22 ↔ (7.4)** `boot <- replicate(N, mean(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))` | (7.4) $X^*_1, \dots, X^*_n$ drawn with replacement from $x$ | Efron's route: resample the 25 numbers already held, 100,000 times. No formula, no $\sigma$, no imagined data. | | **L23 ↔ (7.5)** `sd(boot)` | (7.5) $\sqrt{\dfrac{n-1}{n}} \cdot \dfrac{s}{\sqrt n}$ | prints 0.3035 against 0.3038 — ratio 0.979, which is $\sqrt{(n-1)/n} = 0.9798$: the bootstrap reproduces the plug-in, low by exactly that finite-sample factor. | | **L24 ↔ (7.6)** `mean(abs(means - mu) <= 1.96 * se_exact)` | (7.6) $\Pr\big(\lvert \bar X - \mu \rvert \le 1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt n\big) \approx 0.95$ | prints 95.11 per cent. Not the derivation: a distance becomes a probability only with the shape of the scatter (§5.3, §5.5), and the check borrows `means` from band 6. | ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Where this comes from **The derivation.** Casella & Berger, *Statistical Inference*, 2nd ed., §5.2. Lemma 5.2.5 (p. 213) states $\operatorname{Var}\big(\sum g(X_i)\big)=n\operatorname{Var}g(X_1)$; its proof writes the variance as the expectation of a squared sum and counts $n$ diagonal and $n(n-1)$ cross terms. Theorem 4.5.5 makes each cross term a covariance; independence makes it zero. Theorem 5.2.6(b) (p. 214) takes $g(x)=x/n$, giving $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=n\cdot\sigma^2/n^2=\sigma^2/n$. Bands 2 to 5 are that proof with the expectations written out instead of cited, so that L12 is visibly the step where independence enters and nowhere else. **The name.** §5.2 stops at the variance. The words "standard error" do not occur until §10.1.4, "Bootstrap Standard Errors", p. 478. Taking the square root — (5.2) — is the step every applied text adds and this one does not. **The bootstrap.** Efron, B. (1979), "Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife", *Annals of Statistics* 7(1), 1–26. For the mean, the variance of the resampling distribution is exactly $\frac{n-1}{n}\cdot\frac{s^2}{n}$, not approximately so, which is where the $\sqrt{(n-1)/n}$ in (7.5) comes from and why band 7 can predict the bootstrap's shortfall before running it. **The code.** One chunk, `include: false`, labelled `se-bands`. Every number in the table is pulled from it as an inline `r` expression formatted to four significant figures; none is typed. `set.seed(7)` fixes the single sample in bands 2, 3 and 7, and `set.seed(11)` the 100,000 replicates in bands 4, 6 and 7, so the printed values are stable across renders. The scaling check in (7.2) uses `N_scale <- 2e4` rather than `N`, because each of its repeats draws up to sixteen times as many numbers for a claim that is only a ratio; 20,000 repeats pin the ratio to three digits at a tenth of the cost. **About the sample in band 3.** It is not typical, and it is not tuned. 66.76 against an expectation of 42.28 is roughly two standard deviations high. That gap is left in deliberately: it is the cleanest instance available of the difference between a realisation and its expectation, and a reader who has just seen both numbers in adjacent bands will not confuse them in band 5. The same wide sample is why the plug-in at (7.3) reads 0.31 where the truth is 0.26. **The photograph.** Carl Friedrich Gauss, 1840, by Christian Albrecht Jensen. A faithful photographic reproduction of a two-dimensional public-domain work; the artist died in 1870, and the painting is public domain in its country of origin and in the United States.
